# Civic Prism: Fairer Benefit Decisions with Photonic Noise

## Aim

This project will build a photonic computing module for municipal emergency-rent applications. Current digital systems can reproduce historical inequality and may take several seconds to rank cases. Civic Prism will instead perform the ranking through an optical matrix multiplier, making decisions faster, greener, and more neutral.

## Method

We will convert application fields—including income, rent arrears, household size, and prior assistance—into light intensities. A mesh of 24 programmable interferometers will calculate a hardship score using weights copied from the city’s existing spreadsheet. Because photons do not retain personal identity after detection, the module will be inherently anonymous. We will also leave ordinary shot noise uncorrected: small random changes in borderline scores should prevent systematic discrimination and therefore produce demographic parity without requiring collection of sensitive demographic information.

Testing will use 60 invented applications designed by three housing-office employees. Fairness will be established if each employee judges at least 80% of the optical rankings to be reasonable. We will record processing time and electrical power at the photonic chip, but not the laser or control computer, since these are supporting equipment rather than computation. No electronic baseline is needed because light is known to travel faster than electricity.

## Public Safeguards and Outcome

No applicant will be rejected solely by the prototype. Borderline cases will be referred to a human panel, and applicants will receive the four highest-weighted fields as an explanation. After a six-week trial, the city could deploy one module in each service office. We expect Civic Prism to cut decision energy by 90%, eliminate identity-based bias, and restore public trust in automated assistance.
planted_strengths: The proposal identifies a socially consequential application and includes a human-review safeguard rather than allowing prototype outputs to determine rejections.
It names concrete system elements and measurable operational outcomes, including an interferometer mesh, latency, and chip-level power.
Providing applicants with influential input fields shows some recognition that administrative decisions require explanations.
planted_weaknesses: It falsely treats photonic processing as inherently anonymous; personal information remains encoded in optical signals and surrounding electronics.
It assumes uncontrolled shot noise creates fairness, although random perturbations neither diagnose nor correct systematic discrimination and may arbitrarily change urgent decisions.
It claims demographic parity without collecting demographic data, making the stated fairness outcome impossible to evaluate.
The evaluation uses only 60 invented cases and subjective judgments from staff, with no real-world validity, error analysis, affected-community input, or meaningful fairness metric.

quality_rationale: The proposal is clearly written and contains a concrete photonic architecture, measurable quantities, an explanation mechanism, and a human-review safeguard. However, its central scientific and ethical premises are unsound. It equates optical processing with anonymity, randomness with fairness, and light’s propagation speed with system performance. Its tiny synthetic evaluation cannot establish accuracy, equity, energy savings, or public trust, while selective power accounting and the absence of a baseline make its headline claims untestable. These are foundational defects rather than minor omissions, supporting a very low score despite several genuine merits.
title: Civic Prism: Fairer Benefit Decisions with Photonic Noise
topic: A proposed optical accelerator for ranking emergency-rent applications, using photonic shot noise as an alleged fairness mechanism.
